clinicalPearls: Faciobrachial dystonic seizures (very brief, frequent, unilateral face-and-arm jerks) are pathognomonic and often precede overt limbic encephalitis, offering a window to treat before cognitive damage.
Presents as a subacute limbic syndrome with prominent short-term memory loss, confusion, temporal-lobe seizures and behavioural change, typically in older adults with a male predominance.
Hyponatraemia is characteristic and common, reflecting a syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and its presence in a limbic encephalitis should raise suspicion of LGI1.
The antibody targets a secreted neuronal protein within the former voltage-gated potassium channel complex, so testing serum in addition to cerebrospinal fluid improves detection.
It is predominantly non-paraneoplastic; thymoma is the tumour occasionally associated, so screening is warranted but malignancy is the exception rather than the rule.
Sleep disturbance, hyponatraemia, myoclonus-like movements and rapid cognitive decline in an older patient form a recognisable clinical gestalt.
Immunotherapy responsiveness is high, particularly when faciobrachial dystonic seizures are treated early, and these seizures respond poorly to antiseizure drugs alone.
The condition is strongly linked to specific HLA class II alleles, underscoring a genetically-influenced autoimmune mechanism.
reference.pathophysiology: Leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 (LGI1) is a secreted synaptic protein that bridges presynaptic ADAM23 and postsynaptic ADAM22, stabilising the trans-synaptic complex that regulates AMPA-receptor clustering and voltage-gated potassium (Kv1) channel function. Pathogenic IgG4-predominant autoantibodies bind LGI1 and disrupt this scaffold, uncoupling the ADAM22-ADAM23 interaction and reducing synaptic AMPA receptors and potassium-channel-mediated dampening of excitability. The result is neuronal hyperexcitability manifesting as seizures alongside dysfunction of hippocampal and limbic circuits that underpins amnesia. Because the dominant IgG4 subclass is largely non-complement-fixing and non-internalising, injury is thought to arise chiefly from functional blockade of protein-protein interactions rather than overt neuronal destruction, which helps explain the frequent reversibility with immunotherapy; however, a coexisting IgG1 fraction and secondary hippocampal atrophy can contribute to persistent memory deficits. A strong association with HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQ alleles points to antigen-specific T-cell help driving the antibody response.
additionalDifferentials: Herpes simplex and other viral encephalitides
Other antibody-mediated limbic encephalitides (GABA-B, AMPA, Hu-associated)
Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive dementias
Metabolic or toxic encephalopathy including hyponatraemic encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Serum and cerebrospinal fluid cell-based assay for LGI1 IgG (serum often more sensitive)
Brain MRI with attention to medial temporal (hippocampal) signal change and later atrophy
Electroencephalography, including capture of faciobrachial dystonic seizures and temporal ictal activity
Serum sodium and osmolality to detect inappropriate antidiuresis
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis for pleocytosis, oligoclonal bands and to exclude infection
Cross-sectional imaging of the chest to screen for thymoma
Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment to quantify and track memory impairment
redFlags: Very frequent brief faciobrachial dystonic seizures signalling opportunity for urgent immunotherapy
Rapidly progressive amnesia or confusion in an older adult
Refractory or symptomatic hyponatraemia with neurological deterioration
Status epilepticus or seizures unresponsive to standard antiseizure drugs
New behavioural or psychiatric change with autonomic or sleep disturbance
reference.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with prompt immunotherapy, and early treatment of faciobrachial dystonic seizures can prevent progression to fixed cognitive impairment. Nonetheless residual memory deficits and hippocampal atrophy are common, and relapses occur in a meaningful minority.
pitfalls: Dismissing faciobrachial dystonic seizures as tics, myoclonus or psychogenic movements and delaying immunotherapy
Relying on cerebrospinal fluid alone, since LGI1 antibodies may be detectable only in serum
Reporting a legacy voltage-gated potassium channel result without confirming the specific LGI1 (or CASPR2) target
Attributing the hyponatraemia solely to drugs or other causes and missing the diagnostic clue
Assuming a paraneoplastic cause and over-investigating for malignancy when most cases are non-paraneoplastic
references: Autoimmune encephalitis diagnostic and management consensus guidance
management: Prompt immunotherapy with corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin or plasma exchange, to which most patients respond well
Treat faciobrachial dystonic seizures with early immunotherapy rather than antiseizure medication alone, aiming to prevent progression to fixed cognitive impairment
Identify and correct hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuresis with fluid restriction
Antiseizure medication for temporal-lobe seizures as an adjunct
Screen for the occasional associated thymoma with cross-sectional chest imaging
Maintenance immunotherapy and surveillance for relapse, with cognitive rehabilitation and multidisciplinary follow-up
